Sample Size Necessary for the Accuracy in Parameter Estimation Approach for a Standardized Regression Coefficient of Interest

Source: R/ss_aipe_src.R
ss_aipe_src.Rd

Plans the sample size from the accuracy in parameter estimation (AIPE) approach for a standardized regression coefficient of interest: the smallest N at which the confidence interval for the coefficient, computed at the expected values of the sample squared multiple correlations, is no wider than width, or, with assurance, the published approximation for an interval no wider than width with at least that probability or, by simulation, the smallest N at which it is. Two intervals can be planned for. The default (noncentral = TRUE) is the noncentral t interval for the standardized coefficient, the interval ci_src reports; noncentral = FALSE is the central t interval of Kelley and Maxwell (2003, Equation 1), the interval of ci_reg_coef with noncentral = FALSE for standardized data. For the coefficient in the units of the data use ss_aipe_rc.

Usage

ss_aipe_src(
  true_R2_Y_X = NULL,
  true_R2_j_X_without_j = NULL,
  p = NULL,
  true_std_reg_coef_j = NULL,
  width,
  which_width = "Full",
  true_sd_Y = 1,
  true_sd_X = 1,
  true_cor_XX = NULL,
  true_cor_YX = NULL,
  which_predictor = NULL,
  alpha_lower = NULL,
  alpha_upper = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  assurance = NULL,
  noncentral = TRUE,
  assurance_method = c("analytic", "simulation"),
  G = 20000,
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

true_R2_Y_X

Population value of the squared multiple correlation coefficient

true_R2_j_X_without_j

Population value of the squared multiple correlation coefficient predicting the jth predictor variable from the remaining p-1 predictor variables

p

The number of predictor variables

true_std_reg_coef_j

Population value of the standardized regression coefficient for the jth predictor variable (the predictor of interest)

width

The desired width of the confidence interval

which_width

Which width ("Full", "Lower", or "Upper") the width refers to (at present, only "Full" can be specified)

true_sd_Y

The population standard deviation of Y (i.e., the dependent variable). It must be 1 (the default): the plan is for the standardized coefficient. Use ss_aipe_rc for the coefficient in the units of the data.

true_sd_X

The population standard deviation of the jth X variable (i.e., the predictor variable of interest). It must be 1 (the default), as true_sd_Y must.

true_cor_XX

Population correlation matrix for the p predictor variables

true_cor_YX

Population p length vector of correlation between the dependent variable (Y) and the p independent variables

which_predictor

Identifies which of the p predictors is of interest

alpha_lower

Type I error rate for the lower confidence interval limit, at least 1e-9 and at most .5; a tail area below 1e-9 is refused, as in ss_aipe_reg_coef

alpha_upper

Type I error rate for the upper confidence interval limit, at least 1e-9 and at most .5

conf_level

Desired level of confidence for the computed interval (i.e., 1 - the Type I error rate); a level above .999999998, whose tail areas are below 1e-9, is refused

assurance

Optional probability with which the realized confidence interval is to be no wider than width; when NULL (the default) the plan is for the width of the interval at the expected values of the sample squared multiple correlations (see ss_aipe_reg_coef), not for the mean width over samples

noncentral

TRUE (the default) plans for the noncentral t interval for the standardized coefficient, the interval of ci_src; FALSE plans for the central t interval of Kelley and Maxwell (2003, Equation 1), the estimate plus and minus the t quantiles of its two tails times the standard error formed from the two sample squared multiple correlations.

assurance_method

How the plan with assurance is made, used only with assurance. Neither interval has an exact form for the probability that it is no wider than width. "analytic" (the default), computed without simulation, is the published approximation: that of MBESS for the noncentral interval, and the chi square approximation of Kelley and Maxwell (2003, Equation 3) for the central one; neither computes that probability (assurance_attained is NA), and either can attain more or less than assurance. "simulation" is the smallest sample size, at or above the plan without assurance, at which the probability estimated from G simulated samples is at least assurance, and reports that estimate as assurance_attained (see Details).

G

Number of simulated samples at each sample size the assurance step tries, and in its final estimate of the attained probability; a whole number of at least 100 (default 20000). Used and checked only with assurance and assurance_method = "simulation"

seed

Optional single number. When given, the assurance step is reproducible, and the random number stream of the calling session is left as it was. With NULL (the default) the draws come from the session's current stream. Used only where G is

Value

A data.frame with columns term and value: necessary_N, the necessary total sample size; with assurance, the rows assurance and assurance_attained, which is NA for the published approximation of assurance_method = "analytic" and, with "simulation", the simulated probability at necessary_N that the realized interval is no wider than width, with its Monte Carlo standard error in the attribute assurance_mc_se and the row G. With assurance the printed footer names the assurance method and says how assurance_attained was found, or that the approximation does not compute it; the attributes assurance_method and assurance_probability ("simulation" or "not computed") record the same.

Details

Not all of the arguments need to be specified, only those that provide all of the necessary information so that the sample size can be determined for the conditions specified.

The coefficient planned for is the population standardized regression coefficient of the jth predictor, \(\beta_j\), the quantity true_std_reg_coef_j stands for; on the covariance structure path it is the jth element of \(R_{XX}^{-1} r_{XY}\), with \(R_{XX}\) given by true_cor_XX and \(r_{XY}\) by true_cor_YX, and a supplied true_std_reg_coef_j must equal it. A condition raised by ss_aipe_reg_coef, which makes the plans without assurance, names the arguments of this function (true_std_reg_coef_j, not true_reg_coef_j).

The interval planned for. Both intervals use the standard error \(\sqrt{(1 - R^2)/[(1 - R^2_{X_j \cdot X_{-j}})(N - p - 1)]}\), formed from the sample squared multiple correlations of Y with the p predictors and of \(X_j\) with the other \(p - 1\), which treats the sample standard deviations as constants (see ci_src). With noncentral = TRUE the limits are the limits for the noncentrality parameter at the observed t statistic times that standard error, and the plan without assurance is the noncentral plan of ss_aipe_reg_coef (noncentral = TRUE). With noncentral = FALSE the interval is the estimate plus and minus t quantiles on \(N - p - 1\) degrees of freedom times that standard error (Kelley & Maxwell, 2003, Equation 1), and the plan without assurance is theirs (Equation 2 with the t quantile, at the expected squared multiple correlations), the central plan of ss_aipe_reg_coef at unit standard deviations, with the t quantiles of its two tails.

The assurance step. With assurance the plan is by default (assurance_method = "analytic") the published approximation, computed without simulation: for the noncentral interval that of MBESS, for a lower confidence limit of the squared multiple correlation, and for the central interval the chi square approximation of Kelley and Maxwell (2003, Equation 3), the plan of ss_aipe_reg_coef without assurance with the variance of the coefficient multiplied by the assurance quantile of a chi square on \(N - 1\) degrees of freedom over \(N - p - 1\). Neither computes the probability it attains, so assurance_attained is NA, and the printed footer says so; both start from the plan without assurance, which can be a case or more smaller than that of MBESS (see ss_aipe_reg_coef).

With assurance_method = "simulation" the plan is the smallest sample size, not below the plan without assurance, at which the interval for the standardized coefficient is no wider than width with at least that probability, for random predictors from a multivariate normal population. The width of the noncentral interval depends on the observed t statistic and on both sample squared multiple correlations, and that of the central interval on the two squared multiple correlations, so for either interval the probability is estimated from G samples drawn from the exact sampling distribution of the sums of squares and products, the same samples at every sample size the search tries, so that the estimate changes smoothly with the sample size. The search assumes that the estimate does not decrease as the sample size grows, which held in every set checked (see "The assurance step" in ss_aipe_reg_coef); assurance_attained is the estimate at the returned sample size, at least assurance, with its Monte Carlo standard error in the attribute assurance_mc_se. The distribution of the width also depends on the correlation of Y with the targeted predictor: on the covariance structure path it is given, and on the squared multiple correlations path the step uses the smallest probability over 21 equally spaced values of it, from the smallest to the largest the three planning values allow (the two ends with \(p = 2\), the only values possible there), an approximate minimum over that range. Give seed for a plan that can be reproduced. This is the simulation Kelley and Maxwell (2008, pp. 186–187) described for the standardized coefficient, for which they wrote that no satisfactory method then existed.

The central interval for the standardized coefficient is not the central interval for the coefficient in the units of the data that ss_aipe_reg_coef plans for with noncentral = FALSE, and the exact probability that planner computes is that of the interval in the units of the data. The standard error of that interval is formed from the residual sums of squares of Y and of \(X_j\); that of the standardized interval divides each by the total sum of squares of its variable, which gives \(1 - R^2\) and \(1 - R^2_{X_j \cdot X_{-j}}\), and these vary less from sample to sample, so the standardized interval needs fewer cases to be as narrow with the same probability. For two predictors correlated .3 with correlations of .4 and .3 with Y, a width of .3, and an assurance of .90, this function returns 171 with assurance_method = "simulation", seed = 1, and the default G, at which the central interval for the standardized coefficient is no wider than .3 with probability .914 (.895 at 170). The plan is simulated, so another seed can give one a case away: over seeds 1 to 30, 29 gave 171 and one gave 170. The central plan of ss_aipe_reg_coef there is 187 (.997 for this interval), and the chi square approximation of Kelley and Maxwell (2003, Equation 3, with the t quantile in place of the normal one), the default plan here, is 181 (.986). For their five exchangeable predictors (pp. 312–313), correlated .4 with one another and .3 with Y, at a width of .2 and an assurance of .80, the simulated plan is 478 (with each of seeds 1 to 30; .807, and .797 at 477), where the approximation gives 486 (.877) and ss_aipe_reg_coef 491 (.911). Each probability is the proportion of intervals no wider than the target among samples of raw multivariate normal data (50,000 or 100,000 samples at each N, Monte Carlo standard error at most .0014), standardized and fit by least squares without DMAR. Kelley and Maxwell's own simulation of that example (p. 317) reported 81.64 percent of the intervals no wider than .2 at their plan of 485 (made with the normal quantile) and a mean half-width of .098; raw multivariate normal data give .871 there with the t quantile of their Equation 1 (.887 with the normal one) and a mean half-width of .097 (50,000 samples, Monte Carlo standard error at most .0015).

Note

This function calls upon ss_aipe_reg_coef in DMAR, which plans the coefficient in the units of the data by default, but has a different naming scheme. See ss_aipe_reg_coef for more details.

Warning

As discussed in Kelley and Maxwell (2008), the sample size planning approach from the AIPE perspective used in this function is only an approximation.

References

Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2003). Sample size for multiple regression: Obtaining regression coefficients that are accurate, not simply significant. Psychological Methods, 8(3), 305–321. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.8.3.305

Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2008). Sample size planning with applications to multiple regression: Power and accuracy for omnibus and targeted effects. In P. Alasuutari, L. Bickman, & J. Brannen (Eds.), The Sage handbook of social research methods (pp. 166–192). Sage.

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge. (See Chapter 4 on individual comparisons of means and Chapter 6 on trend analysis.)

See also

ss_aipe_src_sensitivity, ci_src, ci_reg_coef, ci_nc_t, ss_aipe_reg_coef, ss_aipe_rc

design_consequences for what a chosen design delivers: power, the Type S (sign) and Type M (exaggeration) errors of the significance filter, and the expected confidence interval width.

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# Exchangeable correlation structure
true_cor_YX <- c(.3, .3, .3, .3, .3)
true_cor_XX <- rbind(c(1, .5, .5, .5, .5), c(.5, 1, .5, .5, .5), c(.5, .5, 1, .5, .5),
                c(.5, .5, .5, 1, .5), c(.5, .5, .5, .5, 1))

ss_aipe_src(width = .1, which_width = "Full", true_sd_Y = 1, true_sd_X = 1,
            true_cor_XX = true_cor_XX,
            true_cor_YX = true_cor_YX, which_predictor = 1, conf_level = 1 - .05)
#>  term        value
#>  necessary_N 2190 
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# With an assurance of .85: the approximation with a lower confidence
# limit of the squared multiple correlation, and the plan found by
# simulation. G = 2000 keeps the example quick; a reported plan deserves
# the default G = 20000.
ss_aipe_src(width = .1, true_cor_XX = true_cor_XX, true_cor_YX = true_cor_YX,
            which_predictor = 1, assurance = .85)
#>  term               value
#>  necessary_N        2240 
#>  assurance          0.850
#>  assurance_attained <NA> 
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> Assurance method: analytic; the plan is the published approximation, which does not compute the probability that the interval is no wider than the width (assurance_attained is NA) and can attain less than the assurance. assurance_method = "simulation" computes it and returns the smallest plan that attains it
plan <- ss_aipe_src(width = .1, which_width = "Full", true_sd_Y = 1, true_sd_X = 1,
                    true_cor_XX = true_cor_XX,
                    true_cor_YX = true_cor_YX, which_predictor = 1, conf_level = 1 - .05,
                    assurance = .85, assurance_method = "simulation",
                    G = 2000, seed = 113)
plan
#>  term               value
#>  necessary_N        2257 
#>  assurance          0.850
#>  assurance_attained 0.854
#>  G                  2000 
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> Assurance method: simulation; assurance_attained is estimated from G = 2000 simulated samples (Monte Carlo SE 0.008)
attr(plan, "assurance_mc_se")
#> [1] 0.007895695

# The central t interval of Kelley and Maxwell (2003, Equation 1): the
# plan without assurance, and with an assurance of .85 by their chi
# square approximation and by simulation.
ss_aipe_src(width = .1, true_cor_XX = true_cor_XX, true_cor_YX = true_cor_YX,
            which_predictor = 1, noncentral = FALSE)
#>  term        value
#>  necessary_N 2184 
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
ss_aipe_src(width = .1, true_cor_XX = true_cor_XX, true_cor_YX = true_cor_YX,
            which_predictor = 1, noncentral = FALSE, assurance = .85)
#>  term               value
#>  necessary_N        2258 
#>  assurance          0.850
#>  assurance_attained <NA> 
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> Assurance method: analytic; the plan is the published approximation, which does not compute the probability that the interval is no wider than the width (assurance_attained is NA) and can attain less than the assurance. assurance_method = "simulation" computes it and returns the smallest plan that attains it
ss_aipe_src(width = .1, true_cor_XX = true_cor_XX, true_cor_YX = true_cor_YX,
            which_predictor = 1, noncentral = FALSE, assurance = .85,
            assurance_method = "simulation", G = 2000, seed = 113)
#>  term               value
#>  necessary_N        2250 
#>  assurance          0.850
#>  assurance_attained 0.851
#>  G                  2000 
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
#> 
#> Assurance method: simulation; assurance_attained is estimated from G = 2000 simulated samples (Monte Carlo SE 0.008)
